headline: Hot spatula burns, chilli powder in eyes: Chargesheet reveals abuse of domestic worker at former Biman MD’s home

members.title: Hot spatula burns, chilli powder in eyes: Chargesheet reveals abuse of domestic worker at former Biman MD’s home
members.lead: “They used to lock me in the bathroom”, “they burnt my neck with a hot spatula”, “they broke my teeth with a pestle”, and “they used to sprinkle chilli powder into my eyes” — these are the allegations of abuse made by an 11-year-old girl who worked as a domestic worker at the home of Safiqur Rahman, former managing director of Biman Bangladesh Airlines. The girl also said that whenever her father visited her, the family made her wear oversized clothes to conceal the marks of abuse on her body. The police have included the girl’s account in a charge sheet submitted to the court. On 31 August, Rubel Mia, the investigating officer and a sub-inspector (SI) of Uttara West police station, filed the charge sheet with a Dhaka court. It names Shafiqul Rahman, his wife, Bithi Akter, and two domestic workers at the house, Rupali Khatun and Sufia Begum, as accused. . The court has accepted the charge sheet and sent the case to Judge Sohel Rana of the 7th Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal in Dhaka for trial. Rubel Mia, the investigating officer and an SI (Sub-Inspector) at Uttara West police station, told Prothom Alo, “I found the allegations to be substantiated during the investigation and included the findings in the charge sheet. Two of the accused admitted to the abuse in their statements.” The alleged abuse came to light on 31 January, when the girl’s father took her from the home of Safiqur Rahman, the former managing director (MD) of Biman Bangladesh Airlines, and admitted her to hospital. The following day, 1 February, her father filed a case alleging that the accused had tortured his daughter. The case names Shafiqul Rahman, his wife, Bithi Akter, and the two other domestic workers at the house, Rupali Khatun and Sufia Begum. members.title: Sweety spoke to father in Bangladesh before execution in Saudi Arabia
members.lead: Sweety Akter married while she was in Class Eight, but the marriage did not last. After separating from her husband, she returned to her parents’ home with her child. Later, under pressure from her family, she married again. But after her second husband moved to Saudi Arabia, he cut off contact with her. She was at a loss about what to do. Thinking about her daughter’s future and hoping to ease her parents’ financial hardship, Sweety Akter went to Saudi Arabia three years ago. She worked there as a cleaner. But just six months after arriving in the country, she was arrested. Sweety had told her family that several women working with her in Saudi Arabia had illegally purchased a car and that she had been arrested along with them in connection with the incident. Although she was in prison, she remained in contact with her parents. She had told them not to worry even if she could not call for some reason. She last spoke to her father on the evening of 13 October, Tuesday. Two days later, her parents learned that her death sentence had been carried out. Two Bangladeshi nationals were recently executed in Saudi Arabia after being convicted of committing immoral acts at a mosque in the holy city of Mecca. The Saudi Press Agency (SPA) confirmed the executions on 14 October, Wednesday, citing the country’s Ministry of Interior. The two executed Bangladeshis were Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter. .After son’s execution in Saudi Arabia, parents want to see his body just once. Mirzapur Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Zahurul Alam told Prothom Alo that they had learned about the execution of the two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia. . Sweety Akter was from a village in Mirzapur upazila of Tangail. She was the daughter of Md Fazal Mia and Johura Begum and the youngest of five sisters. Visiting Sweety’s home at around 9am on Tuesday, this correspondent found several people gathered in the courtyard, talking among themselves. Some were her relatives, while others were neighbours. …
